listing.title: Yogajee Govind v. Police (1)

text:
Yogajee Govind v. Police (1)

2026 BMB 59

IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF BLACK RIVER
In the matter of:PCN 888 / 2026
Yogajee GOVIND
Applicant
versus
POLICE
Respondent
RULING
[1] The Applicant stands provisionally charged before the District Court of Black River
for the offence of conspiracy to commit a drug offence, to wit, to cause cannabis to
be imported into Mauritius with an averment of trafficking.
[2] On the 10th August 2026, the Applicant moved that the present provisional charge
be struck out on the ground that there is no reasonable suspicion for the continued
detention of the Applicant.
[3] Evidence has already been heard over the course of two sittings and the argument
has reached the stage of the Applicant’s case. The Applicant has made a statement
from the dock following which Learned Counsel for the Applicant, Me.
Mooroongapillay moved to call the Court Manager to produce three documents,
namely:
a. To come and depone in relation to the warrant and detention of the
Applicant. In Court, Me. Mooroongapillay has explained that the
purport of this course of action is to produce the information which
was sworn by the Police at the time of seeking a search warrant;
b. To produce full copy of proceedings of Week End Court (BRC) dated
01.08.26 transferred to Black River District Court in connection with
PCN 888/26
c. To produce full copy of Court proceedings in PCN 888/26 of Black
River District Court.

Page 1 of 6

 [4] In a nutshell, the purpose of the Applicant adopting the present course of action
can be aptly summarised as:
a. To establish certain inconsistencies and contradictions between what
PS 1435 Jeenarain has stated before this present Court in the
present matter and what Inspector Murden stated before the Week
End Court;
b. To establish that at the time the search warrant was sought for, there
was no reasonable suspicion of conspiracy but simply a search
warrant for possession of dangerous drugs;
c. To establish certain inconsistencies and contradictions between what
PS 1435 Jeenarain has stated before this present Court in the
present matter and in the bail hearing in CN 889 / 26;
d. To shed light on the credibility of PS 1435 Jeenarain against whom
the Applicant has made allegations thereby showing that the officer
is not a fair and impartial officer.
[5] Principal State Counsel, Me. Bhatoo has objected to the motion. He explained that
producing the whole court proceedings would be prejudicial to the Respondent as
it might taint the mind of the Court. He added that this further constitutes an
unfairness as the Respondent has closed its case and there is no way to have the
version of the officer on these aspects and to “set the record right”. He went on to
say that the summons ought to have been directed to the Week End Court to
produce the proceedings which occurred there and then. He re-iterated his
objection with respect to the information sworn at the time when a search warrant
was sought before this Honourable Court.
[6] I have anxiously and meticulously addressed my mind to the motion of the
Applicant and the reply made thereafter and the objection raised by the
Respondent.
[7] The principles applicable to justify the maintaining of a provisional charge have
been aptly summarised in Manraj & Ors v. ICAC (2003 SCJ 175) as follows –
“... First, the suspicion should be reasonable: King v Gardner (1979) 71 Cr. App.
R. 13; Prince [1981] Crim. L. R. 638.
Second, reasonability should be gauged not from the personal point of view
of an officer or his subjective standard. It should be appreciated from the objective
standard, the point of view of a dispassionate bystander: Inland Revenue
Commissioners v Rossminster Ltd [1980] A.C. 952.

Page 2 of 6

 Finally, and importantly, the suspicion should be based on facts: King v Gardner
(supra); Prince (supra); Ware v Matthew February 11, 1981, 1978 W. No. 1780
(Lexis). The facts relied on should be such as are consistent with the implication of
the suspect in the crime: Pedro v Diss [1981] 2 All ER 59, D.C.; [1981] Crim. L.R.
236. It should not be equivocal with his implication and his non implication....”
[8] It hence follows that this Court’s task is to assess whether there is reasonable
suspicion justifying the detention of the Applicant. It is trite law that the first acid
test for admissibility is that of relevance. Relevance means that the evidence must
logically tend to prove or disprove a point. It does not need to conclusively
establish the proposition on its own, but it must alter the rational likelihood of that
fact existing.
[9] In the present matter, I fail to see how the information sworn at the time of seeking
for a search warrant is relevant to the present motion. Even if I were to take it to
its highest that the Information was indeed sworn with respect to a simple case of
possession of dangerous drugs, nothing precludes the Police, as the enquiry
progresses, to prefer a provisional charge on a different charge. I am comforted in
my finding by the authority of Ms C. Ramsingh v. The Attorney General of
Trinidad & Tobago (2012 UKPC 16), referred to in Ah Sue v. State (2015 SCJ
11), wherein the Judicial Committee observed that “the lawfulness of continued
detention raises different questions from those relevant to arrest”. It is apposite
for that purpose to refer to the following passages from the judgment which bring
into focus the need for continued detention to be distinctively justified even
following a lawful arrest by the police.
The position after arrest in England is now to be found in Part IV of the Police and
Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (“PACE”): see section 34. Section 37(2) provides
that, where a person is arrested without a warrant and the custody officer
does not have sufficient evidence to charge him, the person arrested must be
released either with or without bail “unless the custody officer has reasonable
grounds for believing that his detention without being charged is necessary to
secure or preserve evidence relating to an offence for which he is under arrest
or to obtain such evidence by questioning him.” As Clayton and Tomlinson put it in
their Law of Human Rights, 2nd edition (2009), at para 10.56, the police must justify
detention on a minute by minute basis.” [Para. 10]
“Although PACE does not directly apply in Trinidad and Tobago, section 37(2)
reflects the correct approach at common law. ...” [Para. 11]
“Was the continued detention justified?” The answer to this question depends upon
all the circumstances of the case. As explained above, the respondent must show
that the whole period of detention was justified. However, while it would be wrong
in principle to hold that, because the initial arrest was justified, it follows that the
Page 3 of 6

 subsequent detention was also justified, it is important to consider the subsequent
detention in the light of the arrest.” [Para 16]
[10] Hence, in the present matter, I am not satisfied that there is any raison d’être
for the search warrant to be produced before me. All what I am tasked of, at this
stage, is to assess whether presently there is reasonable suspicion justifying the
maintaining of the present provisional charge.
[11] With respect to the proceedings in provisional cause number 888 / 26 to be
produced, commonsense dictates that the motion cannot be acceded to. I fail to
see why producing the present proceedings in this present matter is pertinent. I
have gone one step further. Even if I were to find that this were a typographical
mistake and that what is sought to be produced are the proceedings in provisional
cause number 889 / 26, I would still have reached the same conclusion. Learned
Principal State Counsel observed that the present proceedings relate to similar
facts and circumstances in that of provisional cause number 889 / 26 for which a
bail hearing. The short answer to this is that what has transpired in the other cause
number has no bearing in the present matter. Questions of credibility of the
Enquiring Officer ought to be raised at the trial stage. In In Kanhye v The Learned
Acting District Magistrate of the Bail and Remand Court & Ors (2023 SCJ
155), the Supreme Court had this to say:
“Now, it must be reminded that a Magistrate of the Bail and Remand Court
hearing a bail application must be satisfied that the police have
established that there is enough plausible evidence against a person
suspected of having committed a serious offence to justify his arrest and
detention. It must be borne in mind the presumption of innocence and
that it is not the task of the respondent, at this stage, to come to the
conclusion that the applicant “had knowledge that the parcels contained
drugs” and “has embarked on a large scale drug activity”. It is for the
competent trial Court after having heard and assessed evidence
to reach such conclusions eventually.”
[12] I am fully alive that the case law concerns the test to be applied in a bail hearing
when assessing the nature of the evidence but I find no reason why same principle
should not be applied to the credibility of the EO. Contradictions or inconsistencies
at this stage cannot and should not distract this Court from the very goal of this
motion, that is to assess whether there is reasonable suspicion warrantying
continued detention. At any rate, I have had the benefit of seeing and hearing the
EO depose before me and when the Court will deliver its ruling regarding the
outcome of the motion for the provisional information to be struck out, the Court
will assess this. I make no apology to unambiguously state that the present
proceedings should be seen as dress rehearsal as if the case were decided on its
merits. The standard to be satisfied by the Respondent is that of reasonableness.
Page 4 of 6

 At any right, I have not lost sight of the fact of the offence for which the Respondent
stands provisionally charged. I am further alive that it is not at this stage my duty
to assess the strength of allegations levelled against the EO and/or to reach the
conclusion that he acted in an unfair and impartial manner.
[13] For all these reasons, I find that the objection raised by the Respondent has
been well taken and I do not allow the Applicant to call the relevant officer to
produce the documents referred to in the summons.

[14] I would be failing in my duty if I were not to make a final remark. Whilst the
overriding objective that the interests of justice must be promoted or safeguarded
may appear simply to be an explicit statement of the existing objective of criminal
courts, there are a number of elements that are included within its ambit. These
import recognition that all of those who participate in proceedings have rights to
be considered as well as obligations to undertake so as to ensure the efficient
expedition of justice.
[15] This approach was elaborated by the Court of Appeal in Jisl [2004] EWCA
Crim 696 as follows:
“The starting point is simple. Justice must be done. The defendant is
entitled to a fair trial: and, which is sometimes overlooked, the
prosecution is equally entitled to a reasonable opportunity to present
the evidence against the defendant. It is not however a concomitant of
the entitlement to a fair trial that either or both sides are further entitled
to take as much time as they like, or for that matter, as long as counsel
and solicitors or the defendants themselves think appropriate.
Resources are limited. The funding for courts and judges, for
prosecuting and the vast majority of defence lawyers is dependent on
public money, for which there are many competing demands. Time
itself is a resource. Every day unnecessarily used, while the trial
meanders sluggishly to its eventual conclusion, represents
another day’s stressful waiting for the remaining witnesses and
the jurors in that particular trial, and no less important,
continuing and increasing tension and worry for another
defendant or defendants, some of whom are remanded in
custody, and the witnesses in trials which are waiting their turn
to be listed. It follows that the sensible use of time requires
judicial management and control . . .”
(Emphasis is mine)

Page 5 of 6

 M. I. MITTOO
Ag. District Magistrate
This 17th September 2026

Page 6 of 6
